newsitem.title: SPAIN: Chastened Latam investors mainly safer now - IIF.
newsitem.headline: Chastened Latam investors mainly safer now - IIF.

text.p: A top think tank on Latin America said on Sunday the chances of another Mexico-style crisis in the region looked slim but the sheer volume of liquidity flowing into its markets did cause some concern.

Some investors fear that the chance of a U.S. interest rate spike or a major event like the Chiapas rebellion in Mexico in the early nineties, might push the region back into a period of increased volatility in capital flows.

But William Rhodes, who headed the main banking committees during Latin America's 1980s debt crisis,was confident that while problems still remained, much had changed since the Mexican peso crisis broke in December 1994.

"We still have yield-chasing, but one of the differences today is that a number of people were burned by Mexico, and there is now more of a tendency for people to get to know the country where they are putting their money," Rhodes told reporters at a briefing on Sunday before the start of the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) annual meeting.

Now vice-chairman of Citibank and of the Washington-based Institute of International Finance think thank on Latin America, Rhodes said he was heartened by the increasing levels of equity and foreign direct investment over the hot money of the more volatile portfolio sector.

"There is also more in the way of transparency on the part of these countries in the sense of using international accounting standards and being forced to be more transparent in both the public and the private sector," he said.
But he said he was concerned about issues connected with the current high levels of capital in circulation and its implications for the region.
"I've never seen such liquidity in the market as I've seen today -- and that's not just in emerging markets, that's liquidity all over.

"We have to make sure that credit standards are maintained and certain margins are maintained," he said, adding this was a matter as much for the region's individual nations as the banks and the regulatory bodies.
"The countries themselves have a responsibility too in terms of the types of credits they get into and how they use it in their overall economic performance," he said.

Latin American nations have begun 1997 with a vengeance, issuing an all time high of some $12 billion in new debt on the international capital markets in the first eight weeks of the year, and yield spreads over U.S. Treasuries contracted sharply during 1996's record issuance year. --Barcelona newsroom +34 3 424 2659
